parts.context: Two coordinators of a mobile breast-screening service are dealing with a problem before a visit to a small town.

lines: Ibrahim, I’ve just had a call from Wes, the driver. The generator on the screening unit died on the highway last night, on the way back from Riverton.
Died completely? Can’t he get it running again?
He tried. A mechanic looked at it this morning, and it’s a failed control board. They have to order the part from the manufacturer, and it’ll take at least two weeks.
Two weeks. And we’re supposed to be in Elk Lake on Thursday and Friday.
Exactly. Sixty-four women booked, thirty-two each day. And without the generator, the X-ray equipment can’t run. It needs very stable power, or the images aren’t reliable.
Could we just cancel and rebook them for next time?

The next time the unit is in that region is four months from now. For most women, a delay like that isn’t dangerous, but it’s not ideal, especially since some of them waited six months for this booking. The real problem is the six women who are coming back for follow-up images after something showed up on their last screen. I don’t want them waiting four months.
No, of course not. What did Dr. Abernathy say?

She was very clear. She said the follow-ups have to happen this week, one way or another, and that we can spend up to two thousand dollars on a temporary solution, but nothing beyond that without the board’s approval.
Two thousand. Okay. So the follow-ups are non-negotiable, and the other fifty-eight are what we’re trying to save.
That’s how I see it. Let’s go through the options.

qs.q: What is wrong with the screening unit?
o: Its X-ray machine was damaged on the highway.
Its driver cannot reach Elk Lake in time.
Its mechanic has refused to repair it.
A key part of its power system has failed.
qs.ev: it’s a failed control board
qs.x: The generator’s control board failed, so the unit has no power for the X-ray equipment. The X-ray machine itself was not damaged; it simply cannot run without stable power.

qs.q: Why is Maeve most concerned about six of the patients?
o: They waited six months for this booking.
Their earlier results need to be checked again.
They cannot travel to Elk Lake on Friday.
They have never had a screening before.
qs.ev: the six women who are coming back for follow-up images after something showed up on their last screen
qs.x: These women need follow-up images because something appeared on their last screen. Waiting six months applies to some of the other patients, not specifically these six.

qs.q: What has Dr. Abernathy decided?
o: The follow-up patients must be seen this week.
The board must approve any new spending.
The visit should be moved to next month.
The unit should be repaired whatever the cost.
qs.ev: She said the follow-ups have to happen this week, one way or another
qs.x: She insists the follow-ups happen this week. Board approval is needed only for spending above $2,000, not for any spending at all.

lines: What about renting a generator? There must be construction companies near Elk Lake with big ones.
I checked. The only rental place with a unit big enough is in Thunder Ridge, four hours away. Fourteen hundred for two days, plus six hundred for delivery. So exactly at our limit.

Except that when I called the equipment manufacturer, they said they won’t support the X-ray system on a rented generator. Any power fluctuation could affect image quality, and if we get a bad image, the woman has to come back anyway. Or worse, something gets missed.
Okay, so that’s out. What about plugging the unit into a building? It has a shore-power connection, doesn’t it?

It does, but it needs a heavy-duty fifty-amp outlet, and most buildings don’t have one outside. The arena does, but this weekend there’s a regional hockey tournament, and the parking lot will be packed from Thursday on.
Hmm. What about sending the six follow-ups to the regional hospital in Bracewood? They have a full imaging department.

I called them. They’d take the six, no problem. But it’s a ninety-minute drive each way, and two of those women don’t drive. It would work for the follow-ups, but it does nothing for the other fifty-eight.
Wait. What about the fire hall? Fire halls have heavy-duty outlets to keep the trucks and equipment charged. My brother-in-law’s a volunteer firefighter out there.
That’s actually not a bad idea. Can you call him?

qs.q: Why do they reject renting a generator?
o: It would cost more than they are allowed to spend.
It could not be delivered in time for Thursday.
It might produce unreliable screening results.
The rental company only rents for a full week.
qs.ev: Any power fluctuation could affect image quality
qs.x: The manufacturer warns that power fluctuations from a rented generator could spoil images. The total of $2,000 is exactly at the limit, so cost is not the reason.

qs.q: Why can’t the unit use the outlet at the arena?
o: The outlet is the wrong type for the unit.
The Zamboni charger uses all of the power.
The arena is closed for renovations.
There will be nowhere to park during an event.
qs.ev: the parking lot will be packed from Thursday on
qs.x: The arena has the right outlet, but a hockey tournament will fill the parking lot. The outlet type is not the problem.

qs.q: What is Maeve’s view of sending the six follow-up patients to Bracewood?
o: It solves only part of the problem.
It is too expensive to arrange.
The hospital is unwilling to help.
It is the best option for everyone.
qs.ev: It would work for the follow-ups, but it does nothing for the other fifty-eight.
qs.x: Bracewood would accept the six, but the other fifty-eight women would still lose their appointments. The hospital is willing – “no problem” – so the third option is wrong.

lines: Good news. The fire chief says we can park beside the hall on Thursday and Friday and plug into their outlet. They just need us to keep the front apron clear so the trucks can get out.
That’s fantastic. Is the outlet the right kind?
Fifty amps, same as the arena. Wes checked the photos the chief sent. The only catch is location. The fire hall is on the highway, about six kilometres outside town.
Hmm. A lot of our clients in Elk Lake are older, and some don’t drive. Six kilometres might as well be sixty if you don’t have a car.
What if we ran a shuttle? The seniors’ centre has a van, and they often help people get to medical appointments.
That could work. A run every hour from the library, maybe? The library’s right in the centre of town, and everyone knows where it is.
And the six follow-ups? Still Bracewood?

No, if the fire hall works, I’d rather keep them with us. Their previous images are already in our system, and the radiologist can compare them directly. But I’ll book them first thing Thursday morning, so if anything goes wrong with the power, there’s still time to get them to Bracewood that afternoon.
Smart. So I’ll call the seniors’ centre about the van.
And I’ll start calling all sixty-four women to tell them about the new location. Actually, could you also send a text reminder the night before? Some of them won’t answer an unknown number.
Sure, I’ll set that up this afternoon.

qs.q: Why does Maeve want to keep the follow-up patients with the mobile unit?
o: Bracewood has cancelled their appointments.
The patients refused to drive ninety minutes.
Their earlier images can be compared easily.
The fire hall is closer to their homes.
qs.ev: Their previous images are already in our system, and the radiologist can compare them directly.
qs.x: Their previous images are in the unit’s system, so comparison is straightforward. Bracewood remains a backup for Thursday afternoon, so it has not cancelled anything.

qs.q: What will Maeve do next?
o: Arrange the shuttle with the seniors’ centre
Contact every patient about the change
Send text reminders the night before
Book the follow-ups at Bracewood
qs.ev: I’ll start calling all sixty-four women to tell them about the new location.
qs.x: Maeve will phone all sixty-four women about the fire hall. Ibrahim is handling the van and the text reminders.

parts.context: A man is speaking with an employee at a medical supply store.

lines: Hi. My wife, Elaine, had foot surgery on Monday, and she’s not allowed to put any weight on it for six weeks. The hospital gave her crutches, but honestly, she’s struggling. Someone suggested a knee scooter.

That’s a very common choice after foot surgery. Most people find them much easier than crutches, especially at home. We rent and sell them. Renting is forty-five dollars a week, or a hundred and twenty for a month. Buying a new one is two hundred and ninety.
Six weeks… so if we rent by the month and then add two weeks, that’s two hundred and ten. Almost as much as buying one.

Right. A lot of people in your situation end up buying, especially since recovery sometimes takes longer than expected. But if you buy, it’s yours to deal with afterwards. Some people resell them online.
Hmm. Does insurance cover any of it?

Many extended health plans cover rentals but not purchases, or they only cover purchases with a doctor’s prescription. I’d check your plan. If it covers rental at eighty percent, renting would obviously work out much cheaper for you.
I’ll call them this afternoon. In the meantime, can we take one home today?
Sure. We’d need a two-hundred-dollar deposit on a credit card, which is refunded when you bring it back. And I’ll need your wife’s height, so I can adjust it properly.
She’s about five foot four. Is that okay?

That’s perfect for our standard model. The tall model is for people over six feet. One thing to keep in mind: the scooter is great on flat floors, but it’s not designed for stairs at all. Do you have stairs at home?
Three steps at the front door, and our bedroom’s upstairs.

Then she’ll still need the crutches for the stairs, or she might sit and go up one step at a time. Some families set up a bed on the main floor for the first few weeks. Honestly, I’d recommend it. Falls on stairs are the most common way people re-injure themselves.
She won’t like that, but I think you’re right. Okay, let’s do a one-week rental for now, and I’ll switch to buying if the insurance doesn’t help.
No problem. And if you decide to buy within two weeks, we’ll put the rental fee toward the purchase price.

qs.q: Why does Desmond want a knee scooter?
o: His wife is finding crutches difficult.
The hospital told him to rent one.
His wife can now put weight on her foot.
Crutches are not allowed after this surgery.
qs.ev: The hospital gave her crutches, but honestly, she’s struggling.
qs.x: Elaine is struggling with the crutches the hospital gave her. The scooter was suggested by “someone”, not the hospital, and she cannot put any weight on her foot.

qs.q: What does Desmond realize about renting for six weeks?
o: It would be cheaper than renting weekly.
It would be cheaper than any insurance plan.
It would cost nearly as much as buying.
It would include a free resale option.
qs.ev: Almost as much as buying one.
qs.x: One month plus two weeks costs $210, close to the $290 purchase price. Insurance is discussed separately and is not compared with renting.

qs.q: According to Ruth, when would renting clearly be the better choice?
o: If his wife is taller than six feet
If recovery takes longer than six weeks
If he resells the scooter online
If his insurance pays most of the rental
qs.ev: If it covers rental at eighty percent, renting would obviously work out much cheaper for you.
qs.x: If insurance covers 80% of rental, renting is much cheaper. A longer recovery is actually a reason people end up buying.

qs.q: What does Ruth suggest about the stairs?
o: The scooter can be carried upstairs safely.
His wife should avoid going upstairs for now.
They should install a ramp at the front door.
The tall model would be safer on steps.
qs.ev: Some families set up a bed on the main floor for the first few weeks.
qs.x: She recommends a main-floor bed because stair falls cause re-injury, implying Elaine should stay downstairs. The scooter is not designed for stairs at all.

qs.q: What does Desmond decide to do?
o: Rent the scooter for one week to start
Buy the scooter and claim it later
Rent the scooter for a full month
Wait to hear from the insurance company
qs.ev: let’s do a one-week rental for now
qs.x: He rents for one week now and will switch to buying if insurance doesn’t help. He takes the scooter today rather than waiting for the insurer.

parts.context: A woman is calling a blood donation service to ask about donating.

lines: Thank you for calling the donor line. This is Dmitri. How can I help you?
Hi, I’m Priscilla. I’ve never donated blood before, but our office is organizing a group donation next month, and I wanted to check whether I’m eligible before I sign up.
Wonderful. I can go through the main questions with you. First, you need to be at least seventeen and weigh at least fifty kilograms.
No problem there. I’m thirty-four. But I just got back from a trip to Kenya three weeks ago. Is that an issue?
It might be. If you’ve been to an area where there’s a risk of malaria, there’s a waiting period of three months from the day you got back. Do you know where in Kenya you were?
Mostly Nairobi, but we spent four days on safari in the south.
Then I’m afraid you’ll need to wait. The safari regions are considered at-risk areas. So, three months from your return date.
Oh, that’s disappointing. The office drive is on the fifteenth of next month, so I’d miss it.

You would, but you could still go with your colleagues and register as a future donor that day. Then you could book your first donation for when the three months are up. Can I ask, have you had any tattoos or piercings recently?
I got a small tattoo in the spring, at a licensed studio.

If it was done at a licensed studio, there’s no waiting period at all, so that’s fine. On the day you do donate, you’ll have a quick finger-prick test to check your iron level. If it’s too low, we’ll ask you to come back another time. So it’s a good idea to eat iron-rich foods in the week before, and have a proper meal and lots of water on the day.
Okay. How long does the whole thing take?

Plan on about an hour from start to finish. The donation itself only takes about ten minutes, but there’s a questionnaire, a short interview and then fifteen minutes with a snack afterwards. And bring photo ID.
And how often can people give? My husband’s a regular donor, and he says every eight weeks.

He’s right for men – every fifty-six days. For women, it’s every eighty-four days, because women’s iron levels take longer to recover. And by the way, if your husband wants to give more often, plasma donation is possible every week.
Interesting. Oh, one last thing. My son is sixteen, and he’s really keen to come with us next year.
If he’s seventeen by then, he’s welcome. Otherwise he can come along, but he can’t donate yet.
Great. Thanks, Dmitri. You’ve been really helpful.

qs.q: Why is Priscilla calling?
o: To book a group donation for her office
To find out whether she is allowed to donate
To ask about her husband’s donation schedule
To register her son as a future donor
qs.ev: I wanted to check whether I’m eligible before I sign up
qs.x: She wants to know if she is eligible before signing up for the office drive. The office is organizing the drive; she is not booking it.

qs.q: Why can’t Priscilla donate at the office drive?
o: She weighs less than fifty kilograms.
Her tattoo was done too recently.
She spent time in Nairobi last month.
Part of her trip was in a risk area.
qs.ev: The safari regions are considered at-risk areas.
qs.x: Her safari in the south took her into a malaria-risk area, so she must wait three months. Dmitri’s answer depends on the safari regions, not on Nairobi.

qs.q: What does Dmitri suggest she do on the day of the office drive?
o: Donate plasma instead of whole blood
Take an iron test to see if she qualifies
Go anyway and sign up to give later
Bring her son along to register early
qs.ev: you could still go with your colleagues and register as a future donor that day
qs.x: She can attend with colleagues and register as a future donor. Plasma is mentioned for her husband, not as an option for her.

qs.q: What does Dmitri say about her tattoo?
o: It will not delay her donation.
She must wait three months after it.
It must be checked at her appointment.
It must have been done over a year ago.
qs.ev: there’s no waiting period at all
qs.x: Because it was done at a licensed studio, there is no waiting period. The three-month wait applies to her travel, not the tattoo.

qs.q: Why does Dmitri recommend eating iron-rich food before donating?
o: It shortens the time the donation takes.
It is required for all first-time donors.
It helps women donate every eight weeks.
It lowers the chance of being turned away.
qs.ev: If it’s too low, we’ll ask you to come back another time.
qs.x: Donors with low iron are sent home, so eating iron-rich food helps her qualify on the day. Women can donate every 84 days, not every eight weeks.

qs.q: How long will Priscilla have to wait between whole-blood donations?
o: Eight weeks
Twelve weeks
One week
Six weeks
qs.ev: For women, it’s every eighty-four days
qs.x: Eighty-four days is twelve weeks. Eight weeks (56 days) applies to men like her husband, and one week applies to plasma.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a change at a hospital.

lines: Starting Monday, patients at Harbourside General Hospital will be able to name up to two essential care partners – family members or friends who will be allowed into the hospital at any hour, including overnight, and who will be treated as part of the care team. Until now, visitors have been limited to the hours of eleven a.m. to eight p.m., with exceptions only for patients who were dying or for the parents of children. Under the new policy, care partners will receive a photo identification badge after completing a thirty-minute online orientation on infection control and hospital safety. They’ll be able to help with things like meals, walking and personal care, and will be invited to take part in daily rounds when the patient agrees. They will not be allowed to give medications or adjust equipment. The hospital says the change follows two years of consultation and a pilot on its geriatric and stroke units, where it found fewer falls and less confusion among older patients who had a familiar person nearby, especially at night. Vikram Rao chairs the hospital’s patient and family advisory council.

When my mother was in hospital three years ago – she has dementia – every night after eight she became frightened and tried to get out of bed. The nurses were wonderful, but they each had eight other patients. And I was sitting in the parking lot because I wasn’t allowed in. That’s what this policy is about. Families aren’t visitors. We know the patient better than anyone.

Not everyone is enthusiastic. The union representing the hospital’s nurses says it supports the idea in principle, but worries that some families may become frustrated when they see staff stretched thin, and that nurses could end up managing conflicts with relatives in the middle of the night. The hospital says care partners can have their badges removed if they don’t follow the rules, and that nurses can ask a partner to step out during certain procedures. Visitors who are not registered care partners will still be limited to regular visiting hours. During outbreaks of flu or other illnesses, the hospital may limit care partners to one per patient.

qs.q: What is changing at the hospital?
o: Visiting hours will be extended to midnight.
Families will be allowed to give medications.
Chosen relatives may be present around the clock.
All visitors will need photo identification.
qs.ev: who will be allowed into the hospital at any hour, including overnight
qs.x: Registered care partners can be there at any hour. Ordinary visitors still have regular hours, and only care partners receive photo badges.

qs.q: What must someone do to become a care partner?
o: Complete a short course on the internet
Volunteer on the stroke unit
Be the parent of a child in hospital
Attend daily rounds for two years
qs.ev: after completing a thirty-minute online orientation
qs.x: A thirty-minute online orientation is required before receiving a badge. Two years refers to the hospital’s consultation, not a requirement for partners.

qs.q: What did the pilot project find?
o: Nurses had fewer patients to care for at night.
Families preferred to visit during the day.
Patients left hospital sooner on average.
Older patients did better with someone familiar.
qs.ev: it found fewer falls and less confusion among older patients who had a familiar person nearby
qs.x: Older patients with a familiar person nearby had fewer falls and less confusion. Length of stay is not mentioned.

qs.q: What does Vikram Rao suggest with his story about his mother?
o: The nurses did not treat his mother kindly.
The old rules kept families away when most needed.
Patients with dementia should not be in hospital.
Hospital parking lots are unsafe at night.
qs.ev: I was sitting in the parking lot because I wasn’t allowed in.
qs.x: His mother needed him at night, but the rules kept him in the parking lot. He calls the nurses “wonderful”, so the first option is wrong.

qs.q: What concern does the nurses’ union raise?
o: Care partners might spread infections.
Families will receive too much information.
Staff may have to handle disputes with relatives.
Badges could be stolen and misused.
qs.ev: nurses could end up managing conflicts with relatives in the middle of the night
qs.x: The union fears frustrated families could create conflicts that nurses must manage at night. Infection control is covered in the orientation, not raised by the union.

parts.context: Three members of a small town’s recreation committee are discussing what to do with the town’s tennis courts.

lines: Okay, last item: the tennis courts behind the community hall. The surface is cracked badly enough that our insurer says we need to repair it or close the courts by spring. Resurfacing will cost about forty-eight thousand dollars either way, so the question is whether we resurface them as tennis courts or convert them to pickleball.

Well, you know where I stand. The pickleball group has sixty members now, and they’re playing on the gym floor at the school, which they can only book two evenings a week. Two tennis courts could become eight pickleball courts. That’s thirty-two people playing at once instead of eight.
And the tennis players? I know the club’s small, but they’ve been here for forty years. Some of them helped raise the money to build those courts in the first place.
I’m not saying we ignore them. But the club has, what, fourteen paid members? And I drive past those courts every day. Most of the time they’re empty.
They’re empty because they’re cracked and dangerous. Nobody wants to twist an ankle. You can’t judge demand from a facility that’s falling apart.
That’s a fair point, actually. Lachlan, do you know how busy they were before the surface got bad?
The club says they used to have about thirty members, and there were summer lessons for kids. Those stopped three years ago when the instructor moved away.
So we’re planning for the tennis club of five years ago.
Or for the one we could have again. Build it, and they’ll come.

Okay. There’s a middle option I looked into. We could resurface both courts and paint pickleball lines on one of them. The nets are different heights, but you can buy portable pickleball nets. That way, tennis keeps one full court and pickleball gets four.
Shared courts are a nightmare, honestly. In other towns, I’ve seen arguments over who gets the court and when. And the lines get confusing.
I could live with sharing, if there’s a schedule. Tennis in the mornings, pickleball in the afternoons and evenings, something like that.
Afternoons and evenings? Half our pickleball players are retired. They want mornings, same as the tennis people.

Then maybe the schedule alternates days. And honestly, there’s one more thing to consider: noise. Pickleball is a lot louder than tennis – that constant popping sound. The courts are right next to the houses on Birch Lane. In some towns, neighbours have actually gone to court over it.
That’s true. We’d have to think about that.
So now it’s not so obvious that pickleball is the easy win.

Here’s what I propose. Resurface both courts. One stays tennis only. The second gets pickleball lines and portable nets, with a posted schedule that alternates days, and no play before nine or after eight, out of respect for the neighbours. We review it after one season, with real usage numbers.
I can support that if we commit to the review. If pickleball ends up with long lineups and the tennis court sits empty, I want the option of converting the second court fully.
And if the tennis club grows back, I want that taken into account too. Maybe we could use some of the budget to bring back summer lessons for kids.
That’s reasonable. I’ll put both conditions in the motion. And I’ll talk to the Birch Lane residents before anything gets painted.

qs.q: Why does the committee need to make a decision now?
o: The tennis club has asked to give up the courts.
Their insurer requires repairs or closure.
A grant for pickleball courts expires in spring.
The school gym will soon be unavailable.
qs.ev: our insurer says we need to repair it or close the courts by spring
qs.x: The insurer requires the courts to be repaired or closed by spring. Spring is the insurer’s deadline; no grant is mentioned.

qs.q: What is Shauna’s main argument for pickleball?
o: Pickleball courts cost less to build.
Pickleball players helped build the courts.
Tennis lessons for children have ended.
Far more people could use the same space.
qs.ev: That’s thirty-two people playing at once instead of eight.
qs.x: Two tennis courts could become eight pickleball courts, serving thirty-two players instead of eight. Resurfacing costs the same either way, so cost is not her argument.

qs.q: How does Lachlan respond to the claim that the courts are usually empty?
o: Their poor condition explains the lack of use.
The tennis club mostly plays early in the morning.
The club now has about thirty paid members.
Pickleball players also avoid the courts.
qs.ev: They’re empty because they’re cracked and dangerous.
qs.x: He argues people avoid the courts because the surface is dangerous, so emptiness doesn’t show low demand. Thirty members was the past figure; the club now has fourteen.

qs.q: What does Shauna imply when she says the committee would be “planning for the tennis club of five years ago”?
o: The club should be given five years to recover.
The courts were built about five years ago.
Lachlan is relying on demand that no longer exists.
Lessons should restart within five years.
qs.ev: Those stopped three years ago when the instructor moved away.
qs.x: She means Lachlan’s numbers describe the club as it used to be, not today. The courts were built by club members long ago, not five years ago.

qs.q: What is Shauna’s attitude toward sharing a court?
o: She thinks it would work with a schedule.
She expects it to cause conflict.
She prefers it to full conversion.
She believes it would reduce noise.
qs.ev: Shared courts are a nightmare, honestly.
qs.x: She calls shared courts “a nightmare” and mentions arguments in other towns. It is Lachlan who says sharing could work with a schedule.

qs.q: Why does Shauna object to Lachlan’s proposed schedule?
o: Tennis players prefer to play in the evenings.
Pickleball needs more than four courts.
Mornings are too noisy for the neighbours.
Many pickleball players also want mornings.
qs.ev: Half our pickleball players are retired. They want mornings, same as the tennis people.
qs.x: Lachlan gives mornings to tennis, but many retired pickleball players also want mornings. Noise is raised later by Glen, not as Shauna’s objection.

qs.q: Why does Glen raise the issue of noise?
o: Full conversion could upset nearby residents.
Tennis is louder than most people realize.
Birch Lane residents have asked for tennis.
The town has already been taken to court once.
qs.ev: Pickleball is a lot louder than tennis
qs.x: Pickleball’s noise could disturb the houses on Birch Lane, which weakens the case for full conversion. He says neighbours in other towns went to court, not this town.

qs.q: What condition does Lachlan add to the final plan?
o: No pickleball before nine in the morning
A review after one season of use
Consideration of renewed tennis interest
A meeting with the Birch Lane residents
qs.ev: if the tennis club grows back, I want that taken into account too
qs.x: Lachlan asks that growth in the tennis club be considered, perhaps with lessons. The one-season review and the meeting with residents are Glen’s ideas.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about the length of nurses’ shifts.

lines: For most of the past thirty years, hospital nurses in many parts of Canada have worked twelve-hour shifts: three or four long days or nights a week, followed by several days off. For many nurses, it’s exactly the schedule they want, and when hospitals have tried to take it away, they have faced petitions, protests and, in a few cases, resignations. Bernadette Lowry has worked in intensive care for nineteen years.

I’d honestly quit before I went back to eight-hour shifts. With twelves, I work three days a week. That means three commutes instead of five, three days of childcare instead of five, and four days at home with my kids. And for the patient, there are fewer handovers. Every time one nurse hands a patient over to another, there’s a chance something gets lost.

But a growing body of research is raising questions about the long shift. Several large studies have found that nurses working twelve hours or more are more likely to report burnout and to make errors, especially near the end of a shift and on consecutive nights. One study found the risk of a medication error rose noticeably after the tenth hour, and another linked long night shifts to more car accidents on the drive home. Critics also point out that a twelve-hour shift is rarely just twelve hours. With handover, charting and the patient who suddenly gets worse at ten to seven, many nurses routinely stay an extra hour or more, often unpaid. Some hospitals have responded by experimenting with mixed schedules, letting nurses choose eight- or twelve-hour shifts, or limiting the number of twelve-hour nights in a row. Administrators say the flexibility helps with recruitment, but scheduling becomes far more complicated. Others argue that the real problem isn’t the length of the shift but what happens during it. When units are short-staffed, nurses skip breaks, and a twelve-hour shift without a proper break is far more exhausting than one with two. Bernadette agrees with that argument completely.

When we’re properly staffed, I get my two breaks, I eat something, and twelve hours is fine. When we’re short, I don’t sit down for twelve hours and I don’t remember the drive home. That’s not the schedule’s fault. That’s the staffing.

The provincial nurses’ association says it will not take a position on shift length, arguing that nurses should choose for themselves. But it is calling for guaranteed, protected breaks and a limit of three consecutive twelve-hour night shifts. Hospital administrators say they support protected breaks in principle, but warn that without more nurses, they can’t guarantee them. And that brings the conversation right back to where it so often ends up: there simply aren’t enough nurses.

qs.q: Why does Bernadette prefer twelve-hour shifts?
o: She earns more for working longer days.
She finds long shifts less tiring than short ones.
They give her more time with her family.
Her hospital does not offer shorter shifts.
qs.ev: four days at home with my kids

p1.meta: From: Tamsin Reilly | To: Harriet Vo | Subject: Back on my feet (mostly)
p1.text:
Dear Harriet,

Thank you for the flowers and the ridiculous card with the sloth on it. It made me laugh on a day when I really needed to. I’m sorry I went so quiet over the summer. I think you guessed that something was wrong long before I admitted it to myself.

As you know, I went on medical leave from the agency in June. My doctor called it burnout, which sounded almost too ordinary at the time, but I couldn’t sleep, I was crying in the car before work, and I’d stopped answering messages from anyone, even you. Looking back, the warning signs were there for at least a year. I just kept telling myself it would calm down after the next deadline.

The good news is that I’m doing much better. My doctor referred me to a twelve-week group program at the community health centre, and I was sceptical at first – sitting in a circle talking about feelings is not exactly my style. But it turned out to be the most practical thing I’ve done in years. We learned how to notice when stress is building, how to say no without feeling guilty, and, honestly, how to rest without treating it as a waste of time.

I’m going back to work on October 14, but gradually: three half-days a week to start, then full days by December if things go well. My manager has been surprisingly supportive, although I suspect HR had something to do with that.

Now for my favour. A few of us from the program want to keep meeting after it ends, and the health centre has offered us a room on the first Tuesday of every month. We’d like to make a simple flyer so that other people finishing the program know they’re welcome. You’re the only graphic designer I know, and you’d do it in an hour while it would take me a week. Would you be willing? I can’t pay much, but I can offer dinner and my eternal gratitude.

No rush at all – and if you’re too busy, just say so. I’m practising not taking things personally.

Love,
Tamsin

p3.title: The Sunshine Gap: Vitamin D and the Canadian Winter
paras: For about half the year, most Canadians cannot make vitamin D from sunlight, no matter how much time they spend outdoors. The skin produces the vitamin when it is exposed to a particular kind of ultraviolet light, known as UVB, but between roughly October and March, the sun is too low in the sky north of about the 42nd parallel for enough UVB to reach the ground. Since almost all of Canada lies north of that line, the country’s residents depend largely on food, supplements and the vitamin D their bodies stored over the summer. Those stores, held mainly in fat tissue, can last several weeks, but by late winter, surveys suggest that a significant share of people have levels below what is generally considered adequate.

Vitamin D’s best-established role is in helping the body absorb calcium, which is why severe shortages can cause rickets in children and weakened bones in adults. Over the past twenty years, researchers have also investigated links between low vitamin D and a long list of other conditions, including depression, infections and heart disease. The results have been disappointing for those hoping for a simple fix. Several large trials in which people took supplements found little or no benefit for most of these conditions, at least in people who were not deficient to begin with. “Low vitamin D may often be a sign of poor health rather than its cause,” says nutrition researcher Dr. Imelda Santos. “People who are ill tend to spend less time outdoors, so their levels fall.”

Some groups are at higher risk of deficiency. People with darker skin need longer exposure to make the same amount of vitamin D, and older adults produce less of it as their skin ages. People who cover most of their skin, spend little time outdoors, or live in long-term care are also more likely to have low levels. Babies who are exclusively breastfed are usually advised to receive a daily vitamin D supplement, because breast milk contains only small amounts. In Canada, cow’s milk and margarine are fortified with vitamin D by law, and many plant-based drinks are fortified as well, but few other foods contain much of it naturally. Fatty fish such as salmon and sardines, along with egg yolks, are among the best sources.

So should everyone take a supplement in winter? Health authorities in several countries recommend modest daily doses for groups at higher risk, and some suggest that all adults consider one during the darker months. Experts caution, however, that more is not better. Because vitamin D is stored in the body, very high doses taken over long periods can build up and cause problems, including high calcium levels that may damage the kidneys. Testing blood levels is generally not recommended for healthy people without symptoms, partly because results vary between laboratories and partly because, for most people, the advice would not change. In many provinces, the test is not covered by public health insurance unless a doctor has a specific medical reason to order it.

p4.title: Every Teen Should Move Every Day – Make It Mandatory
p4.byline: Opinion | by Dr. Sylvie Arsenault, paediatrician
p4.text:
In most provinces, physical education stops being compulsory after Grade 9 or 10. From that point on, teenagers can – and most do – choose not to take another gym class until they graduate. Many of them will never again take part in regular, structured exercise. As a paediatrician, I see the results every week: fifteen-year-olds with high blood pressure, sixteen-year-olds with type 2 diabetes, a condition we once called “adult-onset”, and an alarming number of teens with anxiety and sleep problems that improve when they start moving.

The evidence is not in dispute. Canadian guidelines recommend that young people get at least sixty minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day. Fewer than one in five teenagers meets that target, and the proportion drops sharply between the ages of twelve and seventeen – precisely the years when gym class disappears from the timetable. I do not believe that is a coincidence.

I am proposing that every high school student be required to take part in some form of daily physical activity until graduation. Note that I did not say “gym class.” I know many teenagers, especially girls and students with larger bodies, have unhappy memories of being picked last for teams or being graded on how fast they could run. If a mandatory program simply means four more years of dodgeball, it will fail, and it will deserve to.

Instead, schools should offer choice. Some students will want competitive sports. Others might prefer dance, yoga, weight training, hiking clubs or even walking. A student who walks briskly for thirty minutes a day with friends is getting real health benefits, and is far more likely to keep doing it as an adult than one who is forced to play basketball. Grades should be based on participation and effort, not on athletic ability.

The most common objection is time. Senior students already struggle to fit in the courses they need for university or college, and adding a credit would squeeze them further. It is a fair concern, and one I take seriously. But daily activity does not have to be a full credit course. Schools could build twenty or thirty minutes into the school day, before first period or after lunch, as several schools in other provinces have done. Research also suggests that physical activity improves concentration and memory, so the time may well be recovered in the classroom.

Cost is the other objection. Schools would need more space, more equipment and, in some cases, more staff. I will not pretend this is free. But community partnerships can help: local gyms, pools and recreation centres often sit half-empty during school hours and might welcome students at a reduced rate. And the cost of doing nothing is far higher, paid later in hospital beds, medication, missed work and lost productivity, by the very same taxpayers who worry about a few extra gym teachers today.

We already require teenagers to study mathematics and English until they graduate because we believe these subjects are essential for adult life. Physical health is at least as essential. It is time our schools finally treated it that way, for every student, in every grade.

t2.intro: Your company has a budget to improve employees’ health this year and is asking staff to choose one of two options.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer? Explain the reasons for your choice.
t2.a: Option A: Adjustable standing desks for every employee, plus an ergonomic assessment of each workstation by a physiotherapist.
t2.b: Option B: Subsidized healthy meals in the staff cafeteria, reducing the price of salads, soups and other nutritious options by half for one year.
t2.model:
I would choose Option A, the standing desks and ergonomic assessments, because they address a problem that affects almost everyone in our office every single day.

Most of us sit at a computer for seven or eight hours a day, and back, neck and wrist pain have become extremely common on our team. Several colleagues have already needed physiotherapy, and two people took time off last year because of back injuries. Adjustable desks would let people change position throughout the day, and an assessment by a physiotherapist would catch problems such as badly placed monitors before they cause injuries.

Cheaper healthy meals are a generous idea, and I would certainly enjoy a half-price soup at lunch. However, many employees bring food from home or work remotely two days a week, so the benefit would be uneven. The subsidy would also end after one year, whereas the desks would last for a decade or more.

In short, Option A is a lasting investment that would prevent real injuries, reduce sick days and help everyone work more comfortably. That seems like the better use of the budget.

t1.prompt: Your friend wants to lose ten kilograms before a family wedding in three months and is planning to follow an extreme diet of meal-replacement shakes and about 800 calories a day. Give your friend some advice.
t1.model: I can tell you’re really motivated, and I think that’s great, but I’m honestly a bit worried about this plan. Living on shakes and eight hundred calories a day might make the scale drop fast, but a lot of that is water and muscle, not fat. And most people who lose weight that quickly put it all back on, sometimes more, as soon as they start eating normally again. So here’s what I’d suggest instead. First, talk to your doctor before you start anything drastic. They can check things like your thyroid and blood sugar, and maybe refer you to a dietitian, which is often covered by work benefits. Second, aim for small changes you can actually keep up. Cutting out sugary drinks, cooking at home more often and adding vegetables to every meal will make a real difference over three months. Third, don’t forget exercise. Walking every day or joining a beginner strength class will help you keep your muscle and feel more energetic. And finally, be patient with yourself. Losing half a kilo to a kilo a week is a healthy pace. It doesn’t sound exciting, but you’d see real results by the wedding, and you’d keep them afterwards.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you made a change in your life to reduce stress. What did you change, and what was the result?
t2.model: About two years ago, I was working long hours at an accounting firm, and during tax season I was completely stressed out. I was sleeping maybe five hours a night and checking work emails in bed. Eventually, I started getting headaches almost every afternoon, and my doctor said it was probably stress. So I decided to make one simple change: no phone in the bedroom. I bought an old-fashioned alarm clock and started charging my phone in the kitchen. The first week was strange, honestly. I kept reaching for it out of habit. But after about a month, I was falling asleep faster, and the headaches became much less frequent. I also started reading before bed again, which I hadn’t done in years. It was such a small change, but it made a huge difference to how I felt every day.

scene.alt: A sunny summer day at a lake surrounded by grass, with mountains in the background. On the lake, two people are sitting in an orange canoe; one is holding a fishing rod. Two ducks swim near the shore. On the left, under a tree, a woman in a purple top sits on a red-checked picnic blanket reading a book, with a picnic basket beside her. In the middle, a man in a red shirt and dark cap is jogging along the shore, and a brown dog is running toward a yellow ball. A sign near the water says “SWIM AREA 10–6”. On the right, a man in a teal shirt stands on the grass taking a photo of the lake with a camera. There is a bright sun and a cloud in the sky.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a lake on a bright summer day, with mountains in the distance and lots of green grass around the water. Out on the lake, two people are sitting in an orange canoe, and one of them seems to be fishing with a rod. A couple of ducks are swimming near the shore. On the left, under a big tree, a woman in a purple top is relaxing on a red-checked picnic blanket and reading a book, with a picnic basket next to her. In the middle, a man in a red shirt and a dark cap is jogging along the shore, and a brown dog is running after a yellow ball. There’s also a sign by the water that says “Swim Area 10–6”. On the right, a man in a teal shirt is taking a photo of the lake.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the dog is going to grab the yellow ball and then run straight into the lake with it, because it looks really excited. It might even swim out toward the ducks, which would scare them away and probably annoy the people fishing in the canoe. The jogger will likely have to jump out of the way, or maybe he’s the dog’s owner and he’ll start calling it back. The woman on the picnic blanket will probably look up from her book to see what all the noise is about, and she might laugh. As for the man with the camera, I bet he’ll get a great action shot of the dog splashing into the water. Later on, since the sign says the swim area opens at ten, more families will probably arrive to swim.

t5.intro: Your workplace will pay for you to take a first-aid and CPR course, and you can choose the format. You have found two options. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a coworker that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Blended course
details: 6 hours of online lessons at your own pace
Held at the community centre near work
Online part must be finished within 2 weeks

other.title: Evening course over 4 weeks
details: Held at the hospital education centre
Missing one class means repeating the course

t5.persuade: Your coworker prefers the evening course over four weeks. Persuade your coworker that your choice is better.
t5.model: I get why you like the evening course, since a class of eight sounds great. But I really think the blended course makes more sense for us. First, it’s flexible. We can do the six hours of online lessons whenever we want, at lunch, on the bus, after the kids are in bed. Then there’s just one four-hour practice session. With the evening course, we’d have to give up four Tuesday nights in a row, and if one of us gets sick or has to work late even once, we’d have to repeat the whole thing. That’s a real risk. Second, the practice session is at the community centre right by the office, so we could walk over after work. The hospital education centre is across town. And honestly, the online part means we can review the material as many times as we want.

t6.situation: Your 15-year-old son plays on a competitive hockey team. Last weekend, he hit his head during a game and was diagnosed with a mild concussion. The doctor said he must not play for at least two weeks. His coach has told him that if he misses the playoff game this Saturday, he may lose his place on the team, and now your son wants to play.
options: Talk to the coach and explain why your son will not play on Saturday.
Talk to your son and explain why he cannot play on Saturday.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hi Coach Bartlett, thanks for taking a minute. I wanted to talk to you about Jayden and Saturday’s game. I know how important the playoffs are, and Jayden really wants to be out there. But his doctor diagnosed a concussion last weekend and told us clearly that he can’t play for at least two weeks. If he takes another hit before his brain has healed, the damage could be much more serious and even permanent. So he won’t be playing on Saturday. I’ll send you a copy of the doctor’s note. What I’m hoping is that this won’t count against him. He’s been committed all season, and I don’t think he should lose his spot for following medical advice. He could still come to the game and support the team from the bench. Once the doctor clears him, he’ll be back and ready to work hard.

t7.prompt: Some people believe employers should be required to give workers a few paid mental-health days each year, in addition to regular sick days. Others think this would be too costly for businesses. What is your opinion? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: I believe employers should be required to provide a few paid mental-health days each year. My first reason is that mental health is just as real as physical health, but many people feel they can’t call in sick unless they have a fever or the flu. So instead, they come to work exhausted, anxious or burnt out, and they aren’t productive anyway. Having a separate, clearly named mental-health day sends the message that it’s normal to take care of your mind, and it encourages people to rest before a small problem becomes a serious one. Second, I think it would actually save employers money in the long run. When people burn out completely, they may need weeks or months of leave, and companies have to pay for replacements and lose experienced staff. Two or three days a year is a small price compared with that. I understand the concern for small businesses, especially ones with only a few employees. Maybe the government could help them with a tax credit or allow the days to be scheduled in advance when possible. But overall, I think healthier, more rested employees are better for everyone, including the business owners themselves.

scene.alt: A park on a walking trail with an enormous wooden chair, about as tall as a three-storey building, standing on the grass. A metal ladder leans against the front of the seat. On the seat, high above the ground, a woman in an orange shirt is waving, and a child in a blue shirt is sitting beside her. On the ground, an older man with grey hair and glasses stands next to a sign that reads “TRAIL REST STOP”. On the right, a woman in a green shirt sits on a normal-sized bench holding a cup. There are two trees, a bird and a cloud in the sky.

t8.prompt: While hiking a trail in a provincial park, you come across this unusual rest stop. Call your sister, describe what you see, and explain whether you think the whole family, including your elderly parents and young children, should come here next weekend. Your sister cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hi Nadine, it’s me. I’m on the lakeside trail, and you will not believe this rest stop. There’s a wooden chair here that’s absolutely enormous. I mean, it’s taller than a three-storey house. It looks like a normal kitchen chair, just blown up to giant size. There’s a metal ladder leaning against the seat, and right now a woman is standing up there waving, with a little boy sitting next to her. The sign says “Trail Rest Stop”, which is kind of funny, because nobody is resting on that thing! I think the kids would absolutely love it, and the photos would be amazing. But I’m not sure about Mom and Dad. That ladder is really steep, and there’s no railing at the top. The good news is there’s a regular bench right beside it, so they could sit there and watch. I’d say let’s come.
